BREAKING: Human rights group KARAPATAN decries torture, 'maximum violence' against PWDs in custody of Manila Police

In a statement, KARAPATAN strongly condemned mistreatment of those arrested during the September 21 protest actions. The rights group also said that the arrested protesters, including several PWDs, were subjected to torture, forced labor, and other cruel, inhumane and degrading treatment.

"According to reports, the PWDs, along with other detainees, have been subjected to beatings, forced to perform degrading tasks, extorted for money in exchange for protection from further harm, and coerced into admitting guilt," KARAPATAN said.

“The MPD should take their hands off the arrested persons and stop their atrocious acts. What makes these violations even more reprehensible is that the victims are PWDs, who should be afforded protection and care—not violence and humiliation. These acts are blatant violations of their rights as persons deprived of liberty, guaranteed under both domestic law and international humanitarian standards,” said KARAPATAN Deputy Secretary General Atty. Maria Sol Taule.

KARAPATAN also received reports detailing how Edzel Santos, a PWD, was beaten, suffocated with a plastic bag over his head, and sustained multiple injuries while in custody. Alexis Bisuyo and Alvin Karingal, also PWDs, sustained injuries during police interrogation.

“Many detainees continue to endure untreated injuries. In recent days, volunteer medical professionals sought by families of the victims were barred from entering the detention facility, further depriving the detainees of urgently needed medical attention. One detainee has a swollen foot at risk of infection, while many others are showing alarming symptoms such as fever and body pains, likely caused by the torture they suffered,” Taule added.

KARAPATAN and other human rights advocates reiterated their call for the immediate release of all those illegally arrested on September 21, as well as a full and independent investigation into what they described as the “maximum violence” employed by police against protesters and detainees.

“The State has inflicted the gravest violence on the poor Filipinos by robbing us of a dignified life, rights and freedoms through corruption, fascist attacks and oppression. The people have had enough. This has to end now,” Taule said.

Photos from KARAPATAN

data.raw_text:
READ: Photojournalists’ Center of the Philippines condemns violence, harassment & intimidation by police vs press who covered the anti-corruption rally in Manila. 

The PCP calls for an immediate, transparent investigation into the attacks on journalists last Sept. 21.

The group cites the case of Zedrich Xylak Madrid, staff photographer of Pinoy Weekly, whom they said was physically assaulted by police officers while covering the attempted arrest of a protester in Mendiola.

“Despite clearly identifying himself as a journalist, Madrid was grabbed and hit in full view of fellow journalists and protesters,” the group said.

Aside from Madrid, other photographers, mostly from the foreign media, were also threatened with batons and riot shields, with state forces telling them to stop taking pictures in the commotion in Mendiola.

“These incidents demonstrate a disturbing pattern of hostility toward the press, reflecting a climate of impunity that emboldens state forces to attack those who document civic unrest,” the group said. | @dempseyreyesINQ

It is through Political Science and Development Studies’ political and economic theories that health can be understood beyond the walls of hospitals, exposing how poverty, policy, and power shape who gets to live and die. Holistic care, then, requires bridging theory and practice, and what connects both is context—context we learn by examining the roots and structures of society. Without this, healthcare is reduced to half-care.

Equally, in an age drowning in misinformation, Organizational Communication becomes crucial. It is plain and simple: effective healthcare is healthcare communicated effectively. Communication majors act as oncologists to the cancers of disinformation and bureaucratic breakdown. Through this discipline, we make sure that policies and health information actually reach and resonate with the masses.

The fields of Behavioral Sciences and Area Studies further enrich this pursuit by allowing healthcare workers to grasp how communities think, feel, and act in relation to their well-being. And where Western models narrowly separate “mind” and “body,” disciplines like Philippine Arts remind us that indigenous and cultural ways of healing treat the person as a whole—mind, body, and soul intertwined. To ignore these traditions is to amputate a part of how Filipinos’ sovereignty to understand health and the self.

To neglect the social sciences is to prescribe half a dose for a nation in need of a full cure. What, then, is the use of a stethoscope if it cannot listen to the cries of society?
